On the other hand, contrary to some of the news reports that I've been seeing, these changes aren't immediate and they're not very specific. Even under the best circumstances, these changes do not provide college athletes with the same kind of freedom and flexibility that professional athletes enjoy. So let's start at the beginning on April 17, 2020, the Federal and State Legislative Working Group issued a final report and recommendations to the NCAA Board of Governors. That report has four recommendations that the working group made to the Board of Governors. Number one, the Board should stress to the divisions, that's Division 1, 2, and 3, there's three divisions of the NCAA. The Board should stress to the divisions that modernization of the name, image, and lightness bylaws of the NCAA has must be accompanied by several different guardrails. And those are, number one, compensation received by student athletes can't be a disguised form of payment for participation in athletics. It has to be an actual genuine payment for the use of the athlete's name, image, and lightness. Number two, schools and conferences are not allowed to play any role in the student's name, image, and lightness activities. Number three, student athletes can't be compensated for situations in which they have no legal right to demand compensation. The next is schools and boosters cannot use name, image, and lightness opportunities as a recruiting inducement. So you can't entice someone to come to a particular school because of name, image, and lightness opportunities that might come as a result of being associated with that school. The next is that the role of third parties in name, image, and lightness activities has to be regulated. And finally, modernization of NIL rules cannot interfere with the NCAA members, efforts, and the areas of diversity, inclusion, and gender equity. Before the NCAA even says that name, image, and lightness is going to be allowed, they've provided a list of things that they want to make sure are not going to be allowed. And then the second recommendation the working group has is in appropriate circumstances the board should consider encouraging the divisions to allow athletes to have social media influencer activity. And in doing that, the divisions have to make sure that they take care to implement all the guardrails that were discussed in the previous section. The second recommendation from the working group is that subject to the guardrails that the working group thinks need to be in place. The board should consider allowing athletes to engage in name, image, and lightness activity or they get paid for that activity, but only in appropriate circumstances. And there's a lot of questions yet to be answered about what appropriate circumstances might be. Third recommendation from the working group is a student athlete ought to be allowed to make money from work product or business activity, including social media content that doesn't involve athletics, participation, or play at all. And finally, the timeline. The board should recommend a timeline for divisions to act so that legislative proposals are fully drafted no later than October 31st, 2020. They voted on no later than January 31st, 2021, and they become effective no later than the start of the 2021-22 academic year. So fall 2021. Three student athletes and a working group of 20 people. This is just my thought, but don't you need more representation from the student athletes or people representing those student athletes than just three out of the 20. The remaining group of people are people from the conferences, commissioners of conferences, athletic directors at universities, and presidents of universities and colleges. All of those individuals have a completely different interest in motivation and being a part of the changes that are made and would have a different set of guiding principles I would think than athletes that are interested in being able to expand their rights in ways that are already being expanded in places like California, Colorado, and Florida. And so this committee, this working group, doesn't appear on its face to have adequate representation of student athletes. And I did see in footnote one to this report, it says the working group would like to extend special thanks to the night commission and several other commissions for their thoughtful input. So in my last podcast, I did an analysis of the recommendations from the night commission. The night commission was also not made up primarily of student athletes, but it did seem like there was more student athlete representation on that commission. And this is just my impression of reading the two reports. The night commission seemed very focused on practical guidelines and implementation. The NCAA report from this working group to the board of governors, it seems very defensive. It seems very reactive and it seems very limited. So you basically have two sports which really provide kind of a different universe of opportunities for the participants in those sports than most other sports. Now baseball is very big in some places. There's other sports that have regional impact and are very popular in certain parts of the country, but overall it's the football and the basketball athletes that really have the most opportunities and very well may be influenced and impacted in different ways because they have a bigger stage that they naturally that they play on. So it will be interesting to see how these rules get implemented in a way that tries to balance the fact that you've got these superstar athletes that have a huge platform just by virtue of the sport that they play compared to all the other athletes and the other sports which have a much smaller platform but are also interested in making money for their name, image and lightness. And I think what we'll find is that there are lots of opportunities for the athletes with that aren't in basketball and football, those athletes will have lots of opportunities to make money and to be compensated for their name, image and lightness in ways that don't exist now. So we're going to make these changes whether they are implemented in their current form or in some alternative form ultimately will lead us to a place where athletes are able to be compensated much more significantly. And without going into a whole lot of detail about those cases, suffice to say that the report does its best to interpret those decisions in a way that's still favorable to the NCAA. The next section talks about the NCAA's current rules relating to student athlete and IEL and this was actually pretty interesting to me because I didn't realize a couple of things. First of all, there's different rules depending on which division you are. If you're a division one athlete, there's different rules than division two and division three. This report and recommendation asks the divisions of the NCAA to make recommendations for each of the divisions rather than some guiding rule that applies to all the divisions. There are already a YouTube sensation or a TikTok star when they're 15 years old and so how do you deal with the situation where that person now is going to be an athlete at a college or university? They've got a name, image and lightness that they've been compensated for for the last couple of years that has nothing to do with college athletics. The idea behind explaining what the current rules is then to show how the rules need to be changed to allow for additional use of name, image and likeness as we go forward. And included in the section there is a set of examples where athletes, student athletes were provided with waivers for certain types of activities that they were engaged in that had nothing to do with their athletic competition. So these name, image and likeness rules are a primary example of something where the NCAA I think realizes that they're not treating athletes the same as the average student. But there are lots of rules that the NCAA imposes on student athletes doing the exact same kind of thing. At the while at the same time, our rules obviously don't allow for that. And the way that the NCAA explains that is that look, things are different. Social media is different. Or in the example of kids that have gotten famous before they go to college, same kind of thing. The NCAA is struggling with how to adapt their rules to allow for this different kind of environment, this different world that we live in where social media allows anybody anywhere to become somebody that would be considered an influencer. So these are people that may not have a very significant, they don't have millions of followers, but they might have a couple of hundred followers, but those followers are people who are very interested in a certain type of activity. And that is where a significant amount of money stands to be made for some of the people for college athletes. If they become a micro influencer, they've got high levels of engagement and they can demonstrate that to sponsors. The next section talks about why significant modernization is appropriate. NCAA is basically admitting that times are changing, things are changing, they're getting beaten in the courts. And so they're trying to adapt as they have to. And if they're going to maintain their current position in college athletics in the United States, they've really got to change. They don't have a choice. So if you know you're going to lose, you know you might as well negotiate the terms of your surrender, right? One thing I think that the night commission talks a lot more about in its report that we don't see as much in the NCAA report is examples of what kind of things would be allowed and not allowed. explicit_propositions.text: The timeline for implementing NIL changes requires legislative proposals to be drafted by October 31, 2020, voted on by January 31, 2021, and effective by Fall 2021.
The NCAA Board of Governors received a final report from the Federal and State Legislative Working Group on April 17, 2020.
The report contains four key recommendations regarding the modernization of name, image, and likeness (NIL) rules for college athletes.
The NCAA must ensure that compensation for NIL activities is not a disguised form of payment for athletic participation.
Schools and conferences are prohibited from playing any role in student athletes' NIL activities.
Student athletes cannot be compensated for situations in which they lack a legal right to demand compensation.
Schools and boosters cannot use NIL opportunities as recruitment incentives.
Third-party involvement in NIL activities must be regulated.

assumptions.text: The speaker believes that institutional fairness and consistency between student athletes and non-athletes in campus life are morally and practically desirable.
The speaker assumes that the presence of only three student athletes on a 20-member working group indicates inadequate representation and undermines credibility.
The speaker assumes that the current NCAA structure systematically disadvantages student athletes relative to peers in broader university life.
The speaker trusts that transparency and public scrutiny of policy-making processes are essential for legitimate reform.
The speaker expects that external pressure from state laws (e.g., California, Colorado) will force further changes beyond the NCAA’s proposed framework.
The speaker views the NCAA’s approach as reactive rather than visionary, implying skepticism toward institutional leadership.
The speaker assumes that meaningful economic benefit for most college athletes will remain modest despite NIL reforms.
The speaker believes that regulatory complexity around NIL could disproportionately affect less prominent athletes outside major sports.
The speaker sees antitrust litigation as a credible threat that compels the NCAA to reform its policies proactively.
The speaker values expert input from diverse stakeholders, particularly student athletes, in shaping educational and athletic policy.
